rows.grounds: not beyond the nature of consciousness
because they cannot be non-conscious and no separate bearer is established

items.question: Why are action and the other powers not different from consciousness?
premises: The powers of action and so on are not more than the nature of consciousness.
They cannot be joined to a non-conscious form.
No separate bearer of these powers can be established.
items.inference: Therefore the powers beginning with action are nothing other than consciousness itself.
uncertainties: The exact force of saṃvidrūpādhikā may be read as exceeding or as additional to consciousness-form.
items.plain_english: The powers such as action are not anything beyond consciousness. They cannot be non-conscious, and no separate owner of them can be proved. So they are of the nature of consciousness.

rows.grounds: in the teaching of the supreme Lord
unlike the unseen principle in the Vaiśeṣika system
a separate support for powers conceived as attributes

items.question: Does the supreme Lord's teaching posit a separate substrate for the powers?
premises: In the scripture of the supreme Lord no separate substrate is taught for the powers.
The powers are not treated like attributes resting on an unseen principle as in the Kaṇāda system.
This rejects an external bearer for powers conceived as mere properties.
items.inference: Therefore the powers do not depend on any separate substrate in this teaching.
uncertainties: kāṇādadṛṣṭivat may allude specifically to adṛṣṭa or more broadly to Vaiśeṣika ontology.
items.plain_english: In the teaching of the supreme Lord, no separate support is claimed for the powers, unlike the Vaiśeṣika view that treats such factors as attributes resting on something else.

rows.grounds: powers such as cognition, action, and will
if those powers were different in that way

items.question: What follows if cognition, action, and will are taken as separate powers?
premises: Cognition, action, will, and the other powers might be imagined as mutually different.
Shiva is affirmed as one.
If the powers were truly separate, the statement that Shiva is one would lack real content.
items.inference: Therefore those powers cannot be ultimately separate from the one Shiva.
uncertainties: The verse states a consequence conditionally; it does not by itself spell out the positive resolution.
items.plain_english: If seeing, doing, willing, and the other powers were really separate, then saying that Shiva is one would be empty talk. So their separateness cannot be ultimate.

rows.grounds: this freedom is nothing but consciousness
and that too, when examined fully

items.question: What is the true nature of freedom when it is closely examined?
premises: Freedom is nothing other than consciousness.
When freedom is examined carefully, it does not remain a single abstract notion.
Its expression culminates in many powers.
items.inference: Therefore freedom is consciousness itself appearing as many powers.
uncertainties: The relation between unity of consciousness and plurality of powers is stated compactly and may invite further doctrinal unpacking.
items.plain_english: So this freedom is really just consciousness. When you examine it closely, it shows itself as many different powers.

rows.grounds: since liberation is the manifestation of the self
therefore such a doubt should not be raised here
an effect arising from a cause
even one who knows that cause-effect relation

items.question: Does knowing a cause-effect relation by itself guarantee liberation?
premises: Liberation is the manifestation of the self.
A mere effect produced from a cause does not define liberation.
Even someone who knows a cause-effect relation is not necessarily liberated.
items.inference: Therefore liberation cannot be reduced to ordinary causal production or to knowing such causality.
uncertainties: The compressed syntax of the second half leaves the exact target of the doubt slightly implicit.
items.plain_english: Since liberation is the self coming to light, we should not doubt it on causal grounds. An effect does not always follow in that way, and even someone who knows a cause and effect is not automatically liberated.

items.question: Is the relation between knowledge and liberation a primary cause-and-effect relation?
premises: Knowledge is said to be related to liberation as cause to fruit.
That causal description is not the primary or ultimate account.
If the relation is not primary, the proposed objection does not hold.
items.inference: Therefore the objection based on strict causality does not apply to knowledge and liberation.
uncertainties: The verse denies primary causality but does not fully specify the alternative relation.
items.plain_english: Knowledge is spoken of as leading to liberation, but that cause-and-result way of speaking is not the deepest truth. So the objection raised on that basis does not stand.

rows.grounds: action is of the nature of knowledge itself
a coarsened form within the self

items.question: Why does action appear so varied if it is essentially knowledge?
premises: Action is in essence of the nature of knowledge.
Within the self, action takes on a grosser form.
Because of that grossening, action appears as manifold and diverse.
items.inference: Therefore the diversity seen in action does not contradict its identity with knowledge.
uncertainties: sthūlatvam may indicate phenomenological coarsening rather than ontological change.
items.plain_english: Action is really knowledge in nature. But in the self it takes on a grosser form, and that is why we see so much variety in it.

rows.grounds: among means that operate through action
distinguished by what is taken in and what is external
because of many divisions and subdivisions, they become countless in detail

items.question: Why do action-based means become countless in their detailed forms?
premises: Some means operate through action.
These means are divided by inner and outer distinctions.
Their divisions and subdivisions vary in many ways.
items.inference: Therefore action-based means become countless in their intermediate forms.
uncertainties: The scope of grāhya and bāhya is compressed and may cover ritual, cognitive, and practical distinctions.
items.plain_english: The means that work through action are split into inner and outer forms, and because these keep dividing into further varieties, they become countless in their detailed expressions.

rows.grounds: because means differ, liberation too would differ

items.question: Does the plurality of means imply a plurality of liberations?
premises: Some wise people suspected that different means would produce different liberations.
The previous reasoning explains why means can be many without changing the goal.
By that reasoning, the suspicion is refuted.
items.inference: Therefore difference in means does not entail difference in liberation.
uncertainties: The verse refers back to anena without naming the exact prior step, though the context makes it clear.
items.plain_english: This also answers those thinkers who worried that if the means differ, liberation itself must differ. That worry is removed by the reasoning just given.

rows.grounds: through different causal modes involving impurity and concealment
as in cases like the destruction of a pot

items.question: Do different causes of liberation produce different kinds of liberation?
premises: Liberation may be described through different causal modes such as destruction of impurity or removal of concealment.
Even when causes differ, the resulting event need not be different in kind.
The analogy of a pot's destruction shows one result reached through different causal descriptions.
items.inference: Therefore liberation is not divided into different kinds merely because its causes are described differently.
uncertainties: The long compound lists causal modes tersely; the exact doctrinal mapping of each member is compressed.
items.plain_english: Even if liberation is explained through different causes, such as the removal of impurity or concealment, the liberation itself is not different, just as the breaking of a pot is one event though described in different ways.

rows.grounds: in the analysis of immersion or penetration

items.question: Where is the threefold division of immersion authoritatively taught?
premises: A threefold division has been indicated.
This division is taught in the scripture named Śrīpūrva.
The supreme Lord declared it in the context of determining samāveśa.
items.inference: Therefore the threefold account of immersion has scriptural authority from the supreme Lord.
uncertainties: The exact referent of the threefoldness is supplied by the surrounding context rather than named in this verse.
items.plain_english: This threefold division is taught by the supreme Lord in the scripture called Śrīpūrva, in the section that explains immersion.

rows.grounds: for one whose mind rests on no object
that immersion is declared to be śāmbhava

items.question: What kind of immersion arises for one awakened by the teacher without object-thought?
premises: A person may be free of all object-directed thought.
Such a person may be awakened by the teacher.
The immersion that arises in that condition is identified as śāmbhava.
items.inference: Therefore the immersion arising through the teacher's awakening in a thought-free state is the śāmbhava immersion.
uncertainties: akiṃciccintaka may indicate complete thoughtlessness or absence of discursive objectification.
items.plain_english: When a person who is not thinking of any object is awakened by the teacher, the immersion that arises is called the śāmbhava immersion.
